title: You can have 100 trading signals and still be making the same bet
author: Alphanet_dogwalker
selftext:
Generating a hundred signals is pretty easy now. Figuring out whether you found a hundred useful things is a different problem.

Say you have a momentum signal, a moving average signal and a volume breakout signal. Different formulas, different explanations. Then you check the positions and all three keep buying the same coins after the same move. This is one of the things I'd want to investigate before getting excited about a big signal library.

**1. Different formulas can produce almost identical trades**

Changing the lookback or adding a volume filter can make a signal look new without changing much of what it buys.

Compare the rankings and actual positions. Where do the signals disagree? If the answer is barely anywhere, adding another one might just increase the size of a bet you're already making.

**2. The strongest backtest isn't always the most useful addition**

Imagine you already run several trend signals. Another strong trend signal might add less than a weaker signal that trades at different times.

That weaker signal still needs to earn its place. Low correlation alone isn't enough. The useful test is what happens to the combined portfolio after costs, with and without it.

**3. Small ranking improvements can create a lot of unnecessary trading**

Two coins have almost the same score. A new feature keeps flipping their order, so the portfolio repeatedly sells one to buy the other.

The predictions might be slightly better. Whether that improvement pays for the extra turnover is another question.

i'd want to see how much of the result survives leaving those near-ties alone.

**4. Five surviving signals might hide thousands of failed attempts**

This is easy to lose track of with automated research. The final report shows a handful of sensible formulas. It doesn't show every lookback, filter and variation that got rejected along the way.

A short formula can still be the winner of a very long search. Being simple to explain doesn't undo that selection.

**5. Remove signals and see what you actually lose**

Take a library of 100 and cut it down to a small set of representatives from groups that behave similarly. Freeze both versions and compare them on fresh data.

Does the larger library improve returns after costs? Reduce drawdowns? Or does it mostly generate more orders and more things to maintain?

That's the comparison I'd find interesting. Especially if someone stripped out most of their signals and found that the portfolio barely changed.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good list, and the point about the number of failed tries behind five surviving signals is the one people forget most. A simple way to see the overlap is to look at the daily positions of each signal and measure how often they hold the same coins, not just the correlation of returns. For the removal test, I'd also check it in the worst months, since overlap tends to show up when markets get stressed and every signal sells together. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to test a set of signals with fees included.
